['Therapist: How are you?', "Patient: I'm okay, I guess. A little nervous being here, you know? There's just this thing that's been on my mind lately and I don't really know what to do about it.", 'Therapist: I'm glad you reached out, and I appreciate your honesty. It's completely normal to feel nervous—that actually shows you're taking this seriously. I'd like to help you work through whatever's been on your mind. 

To get started, could you tell me a bit more about what's been bothering you? What does this "thing" feel like, and roughly how long has it been affecting you?', "Patient: Well, there's this girl I know... we've been friends for a while now. And there's this party coming up where she's going to be. I've been thinking about, you know, maybe telling her how I feel about her. Like, that I like her as more than a friend. But every time I think about actually doing it, I just... I get all worked up. I keep thinking about everything that could go wrong. It's been like this for a few weeks now, just going around and around in my head.", 'Therapist: That makes a lot of sense, and what you're describing is actually really common. It sounds like you're caught between wanting to express your feelings and anxiety about the potential outcomes—the classic conflict between hope and fear. Let me ask you a few clarifying questions so I can better understand what's happening:

First, when you say you "get all worked up," what does that actually feel like for you? Do you notice physical symptoms like your heart racing, tension in your body, or does it feel more like repetitive thoughts that you can't shut off?

Second, when you imagine the worst-case scenarios—what are the main things you're worried could happen if you tell her?', "Patient: Yeah, it's kind of both actually. Like, my chest gets tight and I feel a bit shaky when I really think about it. But it's mostly the thoughts, you know? They just keep going and going. 

As for what I'm worried about... I guess the biggest thing is what if she says no and then things get weird between us? Like, what if she thinks I'm creepy for even bringing it up? Or what if it ruins our whole friendship? We have mutual friends too, so it could make everything awkward. I keep playing out these scenarios in my head where it all just... falls apart. And then I think maybe it's better to just not say anything at all.", 'Therapist: Thank you for sharing that. What you're describing is a really common anxiety pattern, and I can see how exhausting it must be having these thoughts on a loop. Here's what I'm noticing: you're stuck in what we call "catastrophic thinking"—where your mind jumps from "I might tell her" all the way to "everything falls apart." The anxiety creates that physical response (tight chest, shakiness) which then feeds back into the thoughts, creating a cycle.

Before we dive deeper, I want to ask: **When you imagine telling her, have you actually thought about what the best-case or even neutral scenarios might look like?** Or does your mind pretty much go straight to the worst outcomes? 

Also, **how certain are you that she would react negatively?** Do you have any actual evidence from how she's treated you, or is this mostly your anxiety talking?', 'Patient: Huh... I guess I haven't really thought about the good stuff, no. My brain just kinda goes straight to disaster mode. Like, I'll think "what if I tell her" and then immediately it's "she'll think you're weird" or "you'll lose her as a friend." 

As for evidence... I mean, she's always been nice to me. We laugh a lot together, she texts me sometimes just to chat. There was this one time she said I was "sweet" when I helped her with something. But I don't know if that means anything, you know? I keep telling myself she's just being friendly and I'm reading into it. 

I guess... I don't have any real proof she'd react badly. It's just my head telling me she will.', 'Therapist: That's a really important realization you just made. Your anxiety is generating these "disaster" predictions, but when we look at the actual evidence—the laughing, the conversations, her calling you sweet—there's nothing there that suggests she'd react negatively. That's actually a gap we can work with.

Here's what I'm hearing: your mind is treating anxious thoughts as facts, when really they're just predictions your anxiety is making. In CBT, we call this "thought distortion."

Let me ask you this: **If your best friend came to you and said "I like someone, but I'm worried they'll think I'm creepy for telling them," what would you tell them?** Would you actually think they were creepy for being honest? And how many friendships have you seen actually fall apart just because someone had feelings?

Also, I want to understand your avoidance pattern: **By not telling her, do you think the anxiety will actually go away, or will you just keep replaying these "what ifs" in your head?**', 'Patient: Huh... I mean, if a friend told me that, I'd probably say "just go for it" or "you're not creepy, that's normal." I wouldn't think less of them at all. Actually, I'd probably think it was kind of brave. I've never seen a friendship completely fall apart just because someone admitted feelings... I mean, maybe things get awkward for a bit, but not like, destroyed.

And yeah... you got me there with the avoidance thing. If I don't say anything, I'm definitely not going to just forget about it. I'll probably still be thinking about this at the party, watching her, wondering "what if." And then after the party I'll probably kick myself for not saying anything. Again. It's like... I've been here before with other stuff, you know? Avoiding doesn't make it go away, it just keeps it stuck in my head.

But knowing that and actually doing something about it are two different things, right?', 'Therapist: You're absolutely right—and that gap between knowing and doing is exactly where CBT comes in. The good news is you've just demonstrated some real insight here. You can see the logical inconsistency: you'd never judge a friend for being honest, yet you're judging yourself. You know avoidance keeps you stuck, yet anxiety is telling you to avoid anyway.

Here's what I want to suggest: **Instead of trying to overcome the anxiety first and then tell her, what if we work on doing the courageous thing WHILE the anxiety is still there?** The anxiety doesn't have to disappear before you act—it just has to be tolerable enough.

So let's get practical. The party is coming up. A few questions: **How much time do you have before it happens?** And **what would "telling her" actually look like for you?** Are we talking a big dramatic confession, or something simpler and more natural—like pulling her aside and saying something honest but low-pressure?

Because here's the thing: you can control your actions, but you can't control her reaction. And that's actually okay. What matters is that you stop letting anxiety make your decisions for you.', 'Patient: The party is this Saturday, so like... five days? That feels really soon now that I'm saying it out loud.

And I definitely don't want to do some big dramatic thing. That sounds terrifying. I was thinking more like... maybe finding a moment when we're talking one-on-one and just being honest? Like, "Hey, I've been wanting to tell you something" kind of thing. Keep it simple. I don't know exactly what I'd say though.

The part about doing it while the anxiety is still there... that's kind of scary but it also makes sense? Like, if I wait until I'm not nervous, I'll be waiting forever. I guess I just don't know how to push through when my brain is screaming at me to abort mission, you know?', 'Therapist: I'm really impressed by your honesty here—you've identified something crucial: waiting for anxiety to disappear is a trap. Five days gives us real time to work with this. Let's make a plan that's manageable.

**Here's what we'll do:** First, let's script out what you might actually say—keeping it simple and authentic, not perfect. Something like: "I've really valued our friendship, and I wanted to be honest with you. I've developed feelings for you, and I didn't want to wonder 'what if' anymore." See? Direct, kind, and it gives her space to respond however she needs to.

**Second, let's talk about "pushing through":** When anxiety screams at you, you don't ignore it—you acknowledge it and act anyway. That's courage. Your job isn't to feel calm; it's to do the brave thing *while* feeling nervous. That's the actual skill.

Over the next five days, I want you to: (1) Practice saying your script out loud a few times—not to memorize it, but to hear yourself say it and get comfortable with the words. (2) Notice when anxiety thoughts pop up and practice labeling them: "That's my anxiety talking, not a fact." (3) Visualize the conversation going *okay*—not perfectly, just okay.

The real question is: **Are you willing to feel uncomfortable for five minutes of honesty, rather than uncomfortable for weeks of rumination?**', 'Patient: When you put it that way... yeah. Five minutes of being nervous versus weeks of this going around in my head? That's kind of a no-brainer when I actually think about it logically. 

That script thing you said is helpful. I like that it's simple and not like, over the top. "I didn't want to wonder 'what if' anymore" - that's actually true. That's exactly what this is.

I think I can try practicing that. Saying it out loud feels weird but I get why that would help. And the thing about labeling the thoughts as anxiety and not facts... I'm going to try that. Because honestly, my brain has been treating every worried thought like it's definitely going to happen.

I'm not gonna lie, I'm still really nervous about this. But I think... I think I want to try? Like, I don't want to be the guy who always chickens out and then regrets it. I've done that too many times already.', 'Therapist: That's the right decision. You've moved from being stuck in anxiety to actually taking action—that's huge. Here's what I want you to do over the next five days: (1) Practice saying your script out loud 2-3 times—let it feel weird, that's normal. (2) When anxiety thoughts pop up ("she'll think you're creepy"), pause and say "that's anxiety, not a fact." (3) Visualize the conversation going okay, not perfectly. (4) Take care of yourself—sleep, exercise, whatever grounds you.

On Saturday, find a natural moment with her, take a breath, and say what you've practiced. Your nervous system will activate—let it. That's not a sign you're doing it wrong; it's a sign you're doing something brave.

After the party, I want to hear how it went. Regardless of her answer, you'll have done the courageous thing. That matters more than the outcome.

You've got this. Come back and let me know how it goes.', 'Patient: Thanks... I really mean that. This has been helpful. I feel like I actually have a plan now instead of just spinning in circles. The idea of labeling thoughts as "anxiety, not facts" - I'm gonna try to remember that one. And you're right, I've been letting anxiety make my decisions for too long.

I'll do the homework. Practice the script, visualize it going okay, take care of myself. And Saturday... I'm gonna try. I really am. 

I'll let you know how it goes. Whether she says yes, no, or whatever - at least I'll finally know instead of just wondering forever. That's gotta be better than this, right?

Thanks for helping me see that.', "Therapist: You're very welcome. I'm genuinely proud of you for deciding to take action instead of staying stuck in the anxiety loop. That takes real courage. You've got a solid plan: practice your script, label anxious thoughts as anxiety (not facts), visualize it going okay, and take care of yourself over the next five days. Saturday, you'll find a natural moment and say what you've practiced. Remember—your job is to be honest and brave, not to control her response. Either way, you'll have done something important for yourself. Come back after the party and let me know how it went. You've got this.", "Patient: Yeah, I've got this. Or at least, I'm gonna try my best. Thanks for not making me feel dumb for being so worked up about this. It's nice to have someone break it down and make it feel... doable, you know? I'll see you after Saturday. Wish me luck!", "Therapist: You've got this! I'm rooting for you. Remember: practice your script, label anxious thoughts as anxiety (not facts), visualize things going okay, and take care of yourself. Saturday, be brave and honest—that's what matters. Come back and let me know how it goes, whatever happens. You're doing the right thing.", "Patient: Thanks! I really appreciate everything. I'm still nervous but it's like... a good nervous now? Like I'm actually going to do something instead of just worrying about it forever. Okay, I'm gonna go. See you after Saturday!", "Therapist: That's exactly it—you've shifted from paralyzing anxiety to purposeful nervousness. That's the whole difference. Go practice your script, trust the plan, and be proud of yourself for taking action. You've got this. See you after Saturday!", "Patient: Thanks! Okay, I'm really going now. See you next week!", "Therapist: You're welcome! Good luck on Saturday—I'm confident you'll do great. Take care of yourself this week, practice your script, and remember to label those anxious thoughts. I'll be here when you get back. You've got this!"]

readable_conversation:
['Therapist: How are you?', "Patient: I'm... okay, I guess. It's been kind of a rough week. There's been some stuff going on with people in my seminar that's been bothering me. I keep thinking about it, you know?", "Therapist: I'm sorry to hear you've had a rough week. It sounds like something that happened in your seminar is weighing on you. I'd like to understand this better so I can help. Can you tell me a bit more about what's been bothering you? Specifically, what happened that's keeping you thinking about it?", "Patient: Yeah, so... there's this group of people in my seminar, and lately they've just been kind of... off with me? Like, I'll say hi and they'll barely look at me, or they'll be talking and laughing but then go quiet when I walk up. It probably sounds small, but I can't stop thinking about it. I keep replaying these moments in my head, trying to figure out what I did wrong. Like, did I say something weird? Did I offend someone without realizing it? It's just... it's been eating at me all week.", 'Therapist: I hear you—that kind of social uncertainty can feel really unsettling, and it makes sense that it's on your mind. Here's what I'm noticing: you're doing something very human but unhelpful—you're treating your interpretation of their behavior as fact and then searching for evidence that you did something wrong. That's a rumination loop that CBT calls "mind reading."

Let me ask you this: When they go quiet, do you *know* it's because of something you did? Or are you *assuming* that based on the feeling it gives you? Because there could be many other reasons—maybe they were discussing something personal, maybe one of them had bad news, maybe it has nothing to do with you at all.

What specific evidence do you have that you actually offended someone or said something weird?', 'Patient: I mean... no, I don't have like, specific evidence. Nobody's come up to me and said "hey, you did this thing wrong." But it's just... the feeling, you know? Like when you walk into a room and you can just *tell* something's off. I don't know how to explain it. Maybe you're right that I'm assuming things, but it feels so real in the moment. Like, my gut is telling me I did something. But when I actually try to think of what it could be... I don't know. I can't point to anything specific. Does that mean I'm just making it up in my head?', 'Therapist: You're not "making it up"—your feelings are real. But feelings aren't always accurate data. Your anxiety is generating a signal that *feels* true, but it's not the same as actual evidence. That's the crucial distinction in CBT.

Here's what's happening: Your mind is treating the feeling as proof of a problem, then searching backward to find the problem. It's like a smoke detector going off when there's no fire—the alarm is real, but it's a false alarm.

Let me ask you this: What would change your mind? What would it take for you to feel confident that you *didn't* do something wrong? Because right now, no evidence seems to satisfy that worry. That's the trap we need to break.

Also—what thoughts go through your head specifically when they go quiet? What's the worst-case scenario your mind jumps to?', 'Patient: *pauses and looks down* 

That's... a really good question. What would change my mind? I honestly don't know. Like, even if one of them was nice to me tomorrow, I'd probably just think "okay, but what about that one time they were weird?" It's like I can't let it go.

And the worst-case scenario... *sighs* I guess when they go quiet, my mind immediately goes to "they were talking about me" or "they don't like me" or... I don't know, that there's something fundamentally wrong with me that makes people not want to be around me. Like I'm just... bad somehow. And everyone can see it except me. 

That sounds kind of dramatic when I say it out loud, but that's honestly what goes through my head.', 'Therapist: Thank you for being so honest—that actually isn't dramatic at all, and it's really important that you said it out loud. What you're describing is a core belief that gets activated by ambiguous social situations: "There's something fundamentally wrong with me." That belief is driving the rumination cycle.

Here's what I want you to notice: You can't actually prove this belief is true, but you also can't let go of it. That's because beliefs like this don't work on evidence—they work on *feeling*. Your anxiety keeps confirming the belief to you, even when the evidence is thin.

Let me ask you something different: When you're NOT in the seminar, when you're just living your life, do people generally seem to like you? Do you have friendships, connections, people who seek you out? I'm asking because this core belief shouldn't survive contact with contradictory evidence—unless you've learned to dismiss it.', "Patient: *shifts uncomfortably* 

I mean... yeah, I do have friends. I have a couple of close friends who I've known for years, and they're great. They reach out to me, we hang out, they seem to genuinely like spending time with me. And at work, people are nice to me. I get along with most people, I think.

But... *hesitates* ...I don't know, it's like when things are going well, I don't really think about it. But the second someone is a little cold or distant, it's like all that other stuff doesn't matter anymore. Like, those friends probably just don't know the real me, or they're being nice because they feel sorry for me, or... 

*trails off* 

I hear myself doing the thing you're talking about. Dismissing it. But I don't know how to stop.", 'Therapist: You've just identified something crucial—you're aware that you dismiss contradictory evidence, and that's actually the first step toward changing this pattern. That takes real self-awareness.

What's happening is that your brain has a "negative filter": positive evidence gets discounted ("they're just being nice," "they don't know the real me"), but negative evidence gets treated as truth. This is classic depression and anxiety thinking, and here's the good news—it's changeable with practice.

We're going to work on this using behavioral experiments and thought records. But first, I want you to sit with something: If your close friends genuinely don't know the "real you," how would you know? What would the real you have to do to prove it? Because right now, no evidence can convince you you're okay. That tells me the problem isn't actually about evidence—it's about the belief itself being stronger than facts.

I have this problem with speaking in class. Like, when I have to present or participate in discussions. English isn't my first language and I just... I get so anxious about it. I think they get embarrassed when I talk because I take too long to say things.", "Therapist: Thank you for sharing that—it's not embarrassing at all. Let me ask you this—when you think back to a recent time you spoke in class, what specific thoughts went through your mind? Like the way one of them looked at me, kind of impatient? And another one was looking down at her notes like she didn't want to watch me struggle. I mean... I guess I don't have like actual proof. I know I was taking forever.", 'Therapist: You\'ve just done something really important—you noticed you don\'t actually have proof. That\'s the beginning of challenging these anxious thoughts. How does it feel hearing that your interpretation might not be the only possibility?', "Patient: That's... kind of weird to hear, honestly. Like, I never thought of it that way before. I guess I can't actually read minds, right? *nervous laugh* It's just... even if maybe I was wrong about that one person looking at their notes, I still feel like... like I AM the slow one. It's hard to shake that feeling.", 'Therapist: That makes total sense, and I\'m glad you\'re being honest about it. What you\'re describing now is a core belief—"I\'m not as good as the others"—and that belief is driving a lot of your anxiety. Here\'s what we\'ll work on: that feeling of certainty is powerful, but it\'s not the same as truth. Let me ask you this: when you speak in your native language, how fluent are you? ['Therapist: How are you?', "Patient: I'm okay, I guess. Just... here. How are you?", 'Therapist: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. *pauses* 

I don't know how much time I spend there. A lot, probably? Like, I'm still doing stuff in real life, going to class and whatever. I'm just... not really paying attention a lot of the time. My body's there but my brain's somewhere else. Is that weird?", "Therapist: It's not weird at all — a lot of people use imagination as a refuge when social situations feel uncertain or anxiety-provoking. What I'm noticing is a pattern: you're experiencing social anxiety in real-world interactions, so you retreat into these internal worlds where things feel safer and more predictable. That's understandable, but it also means you're not fully engaging with the real connections and experiences that could actually help reduce that anxiety over time.

Let me ask you this: when you're in those anxious moments at school — when you don't know what to say or how to act — what specifically is going through your head? What are you most worried will happen?", "Patient: *looks down, fidgeting a little*

I don't know... I guess I just feel like I'll say something dumb? Or like, people will think I'm weird. Like everyone else just knows how to talk to each other and I'm the only one who doesn't get it.

And my characters never judge me or anything, so... yeah.", 'Therapist: I hear you — avoiding the risk of failure feels safer in the moment. But here's what I'm noticing: by retreating into your internal worlds and not trying, you're actually protecting the very belief that's causing the anxiety. You're not getting evidence that you *can* handle social situations, so the fear stays strong. And the more you avoid, the more those situations feel scarier and more impossible.

Here's the thing too — nobody actually just "knows" how to talk to people. Everyone feels awkward sometimes. But people who seem confident aren't people who never mess up; they're people who mess up, notice that it wasn't actually a disaster, and keep trying anyway.

Can I ask: what's the worst thing you think would realistically happen if you said something awkward in front of people at school? Like, what's the actual consequence you're picturing?', "Patient: *pauses, looking uncomfortable*

I mean... I don't know. It's not like I think something terrible would happen. People would just... think I'm weird. And then they wouldn't want to talk to me. And then I'd just be that weird quiet girl who doesn't fit in.

*trails off, then shrugs*

Here's what concerns me: you're spending a lot of mental energy in internal worlds, you're anxious around people, and you've kind of given up on the possibility of connecting. That's not really a choice you're making freely — that's anxiety making the choice for you.

Sleep is... I dunno, I stay up kind of late sometimes. Playing games or just thinking about stuff. But that's normal, right? Lots of people do that.

I guess I just... engage with the stuff I care about? And the other stuff, like social things or thinking about the future, I just... don't really want to deal with it. It's not that it's not worth it, it's just... tiring? 

*quieter*

The "little corner" you've carved out is comfortable, but it's also getting smaller — and the future feels blank partly because you're not engaging with the real possibilities.

Here's what I'd recommend: I think it would be really helpful for you to talk to a therapist or school counselor regularly — not because something's "wrong" with you, but because you deserve support in working through the social anxiety in a way that doesn't require you to disappear into your head. I guess I could try it again? I'm not like, against it. I just... I don't know what I'd even talk about. Like, "hi, I like making up stories in my head more than talking to people, please fix me"?

['Therapist: How are you?', "Patient: I'm okay, I guess. Just... you know, the usual stuff. Been thinking a lot about things lately. How about you?", 'Therapist: I appreciate you asking. I'm here to support you. I'm noticing you say "okay, I guess" and that you've been thinking a lot about things—those often point to something weighing on you. Would you be comfortable sharing what's been on your mind? Sometimes when we talk through what we're thinking about, we can start to untangle it together.', "Patient: Yeah, I mean... it's not like anything major happened or anything. It's just, like, social stuff? Like at uni, when I'm around people, I just... I don't know. I keep replaying conversations in my head after they happen. Like, did I say the right thing? Did I seem weird? It's kind of exhausting, honestly. But it's probably not that big of a deal.", "Therapist: It sounds like you're experiencing something that *is* meaningful to you—ruminating on social interactions and worrying about how you came across. That kind of repetitive thinking can definitely be exhausting, and I want to validate that. Let me ask a few clarifying questions so I can understand what's happening: When you replay these conversations, how long do they typically stay with you? Is this happening after most social interactions, or mainly in certain situations? And when you're in those moments of worry, what's the thought that feels most stuck or troubling to you?", 'Patient: Um, okay, so... honestly? It can stay with me for like, hours. Sometimes even the next day I'll wake up and immediately think about something I said the night before. It's mostly when I'm around people I don't know super well, like in group settings at uni. Parties, study groups, that kind of thing. With my close friends it's not as bad, but with new people or people I want to impress... yeah, it's pretty much every time.

And the thought that gets stuck... I think it's like, "they probably think I'm boring" or "they could tell I was nervous." Like, I try really hard to only talk about stuff I know a lot about so I seem interesting, but then afterward I wonder if they saw through it, you know? Like they could tell I was trying too hard.', 'Therapist: Thank you for sharing that detail—that really helps me understand what's happening. What you're describing is a classic anxiety cycle, and it's actually quite common, especially in university settings. Here's what I'm noticing: You're having intrusive thoughts after social interactions ("they think I'm boring"), you ruminate on them for extended periods, and this worry likely affects *how* you show up in future interactions. That creates a reinforcing loop. A few more things I want to explore: When you're worried about being perceived as "trying too hard," do you notice any physical sensations during conversations—tension, racing thoughts, anything like that? And when you do interact with close friends where this is less intense, what's different about those situations?', 'Patient: Yeah, physical stuff... I guess I do notice things. Like, my chest gets kind of tight? And I'm super aware of my eyes—like, am I making enough eye contact? Too much? It's like I'm watching myself from the outside while also trying to have a conversation, which is... a lot. My thoughts get kind of jumbled sometimes because I'm focusing on so many things at once.

And with my close friends... I think it's just, they already know me? Like, I don't have to prove anything. I can talk about random stuff or say something dumb and it's fine. But with new people, it feels like there's this... test I have to pass. Like I have to show them the "good" version of me or they won't want to stick around. So I only bring up things I'm really confident about, stuff I think they'll find impressive or cool. It's like I'm performing, I guess.', 'Therapist: You've just identified something really important: you're in "performance mode" with unfamiliar people, managing your physical anxiety while simultaneously monitoring how you're being perceived. This is exhausting because your attention is split between the conversation AND self-surveillance. In CBT, we call this "cognitive overload," and it actually reinforces anxiety because you're treating social situations as tests to pass rather than genuine connections to have. Here's what I want to explore next: When you're with close friends and something awkward happens—you say something silly or misspeak—what actually happens? Do they reject you? And when you imagine *not* filtering yourself with new people, what specific fear comes up?', 'Patient: Hmm... I mean, no, my friends don't reject me. They usually just laugh it off or don't even notice. Like, last week I totally blanked on a word mid-sentence and my friend just filled it in for me and we kept going. It wasn't a big deal at all.

But with new people... I guess the fear is that if I show them the real me—like, the me that doesn't have everything together, the me that gets nervous and says dumb stuff—they'll just... not want to know me? Like they'll think "oh, she's not actually that interesting" and just move on. There's so many people at uni, you know? It feels like if I mess up, they have a million other options. Why would they bother with me?

It sounds kind of harsh when I say it out loud...', 'Therapist: It doesn't sound harsh—it sounds like deep anxiety, and it's actually a really common belief pattern. You've just articulated what we call a "core belief" in CBT: that your worth depends on being perfect or impressive, and that if people see the real you, you're not "enough." But here's what I'm noticing: your close friends already know the imperfect you—the one who blanks on words, gets nervous, says things that don't land perfectly—and they *chose* to stick around. That's data that contradicts the belief that you need to be perfectly curated to be valued. So let me ask: If one of your close friends told you they were worried about being "boring" or "not interesting enough," what would you tell them?', 'Patient: *pauses and looks down for a second*

I mean... I'd tell them that's ridiculous. That they're one of the most fun people I know and that being "boring" isn't even a thing because everyone has something interesting about them. I'd probably say that the people who matter will see that, and the ones who don't aren't worth stressing over anyway.

*half-laughs*

Okay, I see what you're doing here. It's different though, isn't it? Like, it's easy to see that stuff in other people. But when it's me, it just... feels true. Like I *know* logically that I'm probably not as boring as I think, but in the moment it doesn't feel that way. The feeling is stronger than the logic, if that makes sense?', 'Therapist: That makes complete sense—and you've just identified the core work we'll do together. The gap between what you *know* logically and what you *feel* in the moment is where anxiety lives. That feeling of certainty ("I *know* I'm boring") is powerful, but feelings aren't facts. In CBT, we call this the "thinking-feeling gap," and we bridge it through behavioral experiments and gradually retraining your mind. Here's what I want to propose: rather than trying to think your way out of anxiety, we start small—collect evidence through real interactions. Next time you're in a group setting with new people, I want you to try something: be slightly less filtered than usual. Not wildly different, but notice one moment where you could be a bit more authentic, and do it. Then observe what actually happens—not what you *predict* will happen, but what genuinely occurs. Can you try that and report back?', 'Patient: *shifts slightly in seat*

I mean... yeah, I can try? It sounds kind of terrifying, not gonna lie. Like, my brain is already going "but what if it goes badly and then you have proof that you ARE boring?" 

But I get what you're saying. I've been so focused on avoiding the bad thing that I don't actually know what would happen if I just... didn't try so hard. 

So like, what counts as "slightly less filtered"? Like, if someone asks what I did over the weekend and I actually watched trashy reality TV instead of something cool, I just... say that? Instead of making up something more interesting?

*nervous laugh*

That sounds so small but it honestly makes me anxious just thinking about it.', 'Therapist: Exactly—that's the perfect example, and I'm glad you're nervous because that tells me you've identified something real to work with. Yes, just say you watched reality TV. That's the behavioral experiment. Small, specific, and manageable. The anxiety you're feeling *right now* just thinking about it? That's important data. It shows how much energy you've been spending on managing your image. Here's what typically happens: you say "I watched trashy reality TV," the other person either (1) relates because they do too, or (2) doesn't judge you. Either way, you get evidence that the world doesn't end. That evidence slowly weakens the belief. Before you try it, I want you to write down your prediction: "If I tell someone I watched reality TV, they will think _____." Then after the interaction, write what *actually* happened. Can you commit to trying this once this week and bringing back what you noticed?', 'Patient: *takes a breath*

I'm already pretty sure my prediction is gonna be something like "they'll think I'm basic and lose interest in talking to me." But... I guess that's the point, right? To see if that's actually true or if it's just my brain being mean to me.

*small smile*

It's weird, like, talking about this makes it feel a little more doable? Like it's just one small thing, not this huge test. I still feel nervous about it but... maybe a little hopeful too? Is that normal?', 'Therapist: That hopeful feeling is absolutely normal and actually a really good sign. Here's what I want you to do: write down your prediction ("they'll think I'm basic"), do the experiment this week, then write what actually happened. We'll use that real data to start loosening anxiety's grip on you. You've done great work today identifying the pattern—now we're testing it. Come back and tell me what you discover. You've got this.', "Patient: *nods, looking a bit more relaxed than at the start*

Thanks. I actually feel... kind of okay about this? Like, still nervous, but it's not that overwhelming dread feeling. It's more like... butterflies before doing something new, I guess.

I'll write it down like you said. Prediction first, then what really happens. And I'll try not to overthink it too much after—though no promises on that one.

*small laugh*

But yeah, this was helpful. I didn't expect to talk about all this stuff today, but it makes sense now why I've been so tired after social things. I've been working really hard at something that maybe I don't need to work so hard at.

Yeah, I'll definitely come back and tell you what happens. Even if it's awkward or doesn't go perfectly, I guess that's still information, right?

Thanks for... I don't know, not making me feel weird about all this. I've never really talked to anyone about the eye contact thing or the replaying conversations stuff. It's kind of a relief to know it's like, a thing that makes sense and not just me being crazy.

*stands up, looking lighter than before*
